open-question.question: The build is to accept slot values held in files beside the inline [slots] table of a host's settings.toml. How does a definition bind a file to a slot name, and where do the files live: discovered by a fixed naming convention under a fixed directory of the definition, named explicitly per slot in the TOML, or another binding, and at which path? (The binding form and the location constrain each other, so both are asked together.)
open-question.alternative: Binding by fixed naming convention, with no TOML entry: every file in a reserved slots/ subdirectory of the host definition (scripts/hosts/<host>/slots/<NAME>.md) is the value of the slot its file stem names. load_definition skips that subdirectory when it collects templates, validates each stem against the existing slot-name pattern and reserved names, and merges the file values with the inline [slots] table into the one slot map the render and the slot-declaration check use. Moving a value out of TOML is just creating one file with nothing to keep in step, and the host's whole definition still lives in its one directory, so adding a host stays adding one directory. Each value's explanatory comment (today the comment above its TOML entry) has nowhere to go: a comment inside the file would be substituted into the tree, and settings.toml has no entry to sit above. The slots/ name is taken out of template discovery, so no host could template a top-level slots/ path. A file and an inline key with the same name can both exist, so this option needs a rule from the duplicate-handling question.

alternative.id: Explicit file entry in slots table

open-question.alternative: Explicit binding inside the existing [slots] table: a slot whose value lives in a file is written as an inline table, NAME = { file = "slots/NAME.md" }, beside the plain string entries, with the path relative to the definition directory and kept under its slots/ subdirectory, which template discovery skips. The loader accepts either a string or a one-key { file } table for each slot. A missing file, or a path outside slots/, is refused. Every slot stays declared exactly once in one table, so its comment still sits above its entry. A name cannot be both inline and file-backed, since TOML refuses a duplicate key. That makes the duplicate question moot for this form. The loader's "slots.<NAME> must be a string" rule becomes a two-type rule. Each file-backed slot repeats its name in both its key and its path, and that pair can drift through a typo the loader then has to catch.

Explicit binding in a new top-level table of settings.toml, [slot_files], mapping each slot name to a path relative to the definition directory under its slots/ subdirectory (which template discovery skips), for example ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY = "slots/ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY.md". [slots] keeps holding only strings, and the two tables merge into one slot map before the render and the checks. The existing [slots] contract (string values only) stays as it is, and every file binding is visible in one place with a comment site above each entry. It adds a key to the fixed schema that every definition must carry, empty or not. A name can appear in both tables, so this option needs a rule from the duplicate-handling question. A slot's comment may sit in either table, depending on where its value lives.

Binding by fixed naming convention in a tree parallel to the definitions, not inside them: scripts/slots/<host>/<NAME>.md is the value of slot NAME for the host whose definition directory has the same name. There is no TOML entry, and template discovery is left exactly as it is because no slot file sits in a definition directory. The definition directory's rule that every file other than settings.toml is a template stays as it is, with no reserved name and no change to how templates are discovered. A host's definition is split across two directories, which breaks the rule that adding a host means adding one definition directory. A slot-value directory with no matching definition (or a misspelled one) has to become a new failure the build reports. Each value's comment has nowhere to go, and this option needs a rule from the duplicate-handling question.

Explicit per-slot binding in settings.toml (as a { file } entry in [slots] or a separate table), with each path relative to the repository root and allowed to point anywhere outside core/ and hosts/. Two definitions can therefore bind the same file, and a value shared by several hosts lives once in a common place such as scripts/slots/shared/. Any file under a definition directory that a binding names is left out of that definition's templates. Where hosts carry the same wording, it is written once rather than copied, so values that are meant to match cannot drift apart. It brings back cross-host coupling of exactly the kind the milestone retires, along with the Claude/Antigravity identity: one edit can silently change another host's tree. A host's wording no longer lives within its own definition. The loader needs path-containment rules that the other options get from the definition directory itself.

Binding by section within a single per-host file beside settings.toml (scripts/hosts/<host>/slots.md), excluded from template discovery by its fixed name. Each slot is a section that opens on a marker line naming it (for example a heading of the slot name). The section's body, up to the next marker or the end of the file, is that slot's value, and there is no per-slot TOML entry. All of a host's long values can be read and edited side by side in one Markdown file, and the definition stays in its one directory with only one reserved file name. The build needs a section parser and a delimiting rule, and a value can never contain a line that looks like a marker. That matters because slot values are Markdown prose that may carry headings. Where a section ends and how its trailing blank lines are treated becomes part of the format, which overlaps the trailing-newline question. A name can also be both a section and an inline key, so this option needs a rule from the duplicate-handling question.

open-question.question: When a host definition supplies the same slot both inline in its [slots] table and as a file-backed value, what does the build do: refuse the definition, or let one of the two forms take precedence, and which?
open-question.alternative: The build refuses a definition that supplies one slot both inline in [slots] and as a file-backed value, whatever the two values hold. The refusal is a BuildError raised while load_definition reads the definition, before anything renders, and it names the slot and both sources. No precedence rule exists. It matches the build's posture today, where every malformed definition (unknown key, non-string value, reserved name, stray placeholder) is refused at load. Every slot then has exactly one place its value comes from, so an editor never changes a value that the build silently ignores. Moving a value from inline to a file has to happen in one edit, deleting the inline entry in the same change, because an intermediate state with both fails the build. It also adds a load-time rule and an error message that the new build test has to cover.

The build accepts a slot supplied in both forms when the two values are identical after the build's normal reading of each, and uses that value. It refuses the definition, at load and naming the slot and both sources, only when the two values differ. A value can be copied into a file and the build checked before the inline entry is deleted, while two forms that disagree still cannot pass silently. The redundant copy is allowed to stay. It turns into a build failure the first time someone edits only one of the two copies, so the second place to edit is never removed, only deferred. Whether "identical" holds also depends on how a file value's trailing newline is read, which the trailing-newline sibling question owns.

The build accepts a slot supplied in both forms and uses the inline [slots] value, ignoring the file-backed one without a failure. The file acts as a default that an inline entry overrides. The definition never fails over this case, and settings.toml stays the one file that shows which value wins. A reader of the TOML sees the value that renders whenever an inline entry is there. A file-backed value can sit in the definition directory and never render. An editor who edits that file sees no change and gets no error, and --check passes because the committed tree was also rendered from the inline value. That is a silent dead copy, in a build that otherwise refuses every malformed definition.

The build accepts a slot supplied in both forms and uses the file-backed value, ignoring the inline [slots] entry without a failure. The inline entry acts as a default that a file overrides. The definition never fails over this case, and a value can be moved into a file and take effect at once, with the leftover inline entry deleted at leisure. The inline value in settings.toml, together with the comment above it explaining that host's value, can be stale and never render. A reader of the TOML is misled about what the tree carries, and the build gives no signal that this is so.

The build adds no duplicate rule of its own. The file-backed form is bound so that one slot can be supplied only once, for example by making the file reference that slot's own [slots] entry, and TOML's own refusal of a repeated key already catches any second entry. There is no new rule, message, or test case. Duplication is ruled out by the definition's structure rather than detected, so neither a refusal path nor a precedence rule has to be written or documented. It is viable only if the binding form chosen by the File-backed slot declaration form sibling gives each slot a single key. Under a binding by naming convention in a directory, or under a separate table, a duplicate can still arise, and with no rule the outcome would come down to an undocumented dictionary-update order.

open-question.question: A text file conventionally ends with a newline while an inline TOML slot value does not. When a file-backed slot value is substituted into a core/ file, are its bytes used verbatim, or is trailing whitespace normalised, and by what rule?
open-question.alternative:
The build reads a file-backed value as UTF-8 text and removes exactly one trailing line ending (a final "
", or "
") if the file ends with one, keeping every other byte as written, earlier trailing newlines and spaces included; a file with no final newline is used as it stands. No check is added for the file's ending. Files can follow the ordinary text-file convention editors and tools enforce, while a value whose meaning needs trailing whitespace (such as the Codex prompt-opener values that today end in "

" inline) can still be held in a file by writing one extra newline, so the file form can carry any value the inline form can and the rule is one sentence long. The file's bytes and the substituted bytes differ by one invisible character, so a reader must know the rule to tell what a file with two final newlines yields, and a value meant to end in exactly one newline needs a file ending in two, which looks like a mistake and invites someone to "fix" it.

The build removes every trailing whitespace character (all final newlines, spaces, and tabs) from a file-backed value before substituting it, keeping leading whitespace and interior bytes verbatim. A value that must end in whitespace cannot be file-backed and stays inline in settings.toml. The most forgiving rule: however an editor or a stray keystroke leaves the end of the file, the rendered tree is the same, so the file ending can never introduce a blank line or a drift diff into a host tree, and the rule matches how the inline multi-line values are written today (closing ''' straight after the last word). A slot whose value legitimately ends in whitespace — today's Codex prompt-opener values end in "\n\n" — can never move to a file, so the two forms are no longer equivalent and the rule constrains which slots may be file-backed, which is the Inline versus file assignment question's to settle; whether this matters depends on that outcome.

The build removes leading and trailing whitespace (blank lines and spaces at both ends) from a file-backed value, keeping interior bytes verbatim, so a file may open or close with blank lines or a comment-free margin. A value that must begin or end in whitespace stays inline. Gives the file author the most freedom in layout — a blank first line, trailing blank lines, any final newline — with one symmetric rule that is easy to state and test. Silently discards leading whitespace too, which no value needs stripped today and which an indented or newline-prefixed value would rely on, so it widens the set of values the file form cannot carry beyond the trailing-whitespace case for no gain the trailing-only rules lack; whether that set matters again depends on the Inline versus file assignment outcome.

The build substitutes a file-backed value's bytes exactly as read, with no normalisation, and the definition loader refuses a value file whose last byte is a newline (failing the build with a message naming the file), so a value file must be saved without a final newline; a value that needs trailing whitespace other than a newline can still be file-backed. What the file holds is exactly what lands in the tree, with no hidden rule for a reader to learn, and a stray final newline is caught at build time rather than surfacing as an unexplained blank line in a rendered host tree. Fights the near-universal convention that text files end in a newline: many editors, formatters, and git's "No newline at end of file" warning push the other way, so value files are awkward to edit and the refusal will fire routinely; and a value that must end in a newline (the Codex prompt openers) cannot be file-backed at all.

The build substitutes a file-backed value's bytes exactly as read, with no normalisation and no check of the file's ending; keeping a value file free of an unwanted final newline is left to whoever edits it. The least build code and the simplest contract: the file is the value, every value the inline form can express (trailing "\n\n" included) can be expressed in a file, and nothing is ever altered behind the author's back. Any editor that appends the conventional final newline silently changes the rendered tree — an extra line break after a paragraph slot, or a broken sentence where a slot sits mid-line — and the drift gate does not catch it, because the rebuilt tree is what gets committed; the error surfaces only in review of the rendered diff, if at all.

open-question.question: Once both forms exist, which slot values are held in files and which stay inline in settings.toml: every value, only the multi-line paragraphs, or whichever each host definition chooses per slot?

The milestone adds a lightweight pytest of the build's rendering. What does that test exercise, and how does it reach the build code: the slot-filling step alone through an import, a full render of a small synthetic core and definition into a temporary directory, or the real build run as a subprocess against the repository's own core/ and hosts/? (What is tested and how the code is reached constrain each other, so both are asked together.)

The Python 3.9 floor run collects the same tests/ directory as the pinned run but has neither PyYAML nor tomllib, both of which the build imports. How is the rendering test kept to the pinned interpreter: a skip inside the test, a collection rule in conftest.py, a location outside the floor run's test paths, or a change to the floor command itself?
open-question.alternative: The rendering test lives under tests/ beside the tool tests and opens with pytest.importorskip for tomllib and yaml before it reaches the build code, so the floor run collects it and reports it skipped. The exclusion keys on the modules' absence, not on the interpreter version; pyproject.toml, conftest.py, and both pytest commands stay unchanged. Self-contained in the one test file with no command, CI, CONTRIBUTING.md, or CLAUDE.md change, and it keys on the exact cause of the failure (the missing imports), so the skip reason printed by the floor run states why. The skip also fires silently under the pinned run if PyYAML ever goes missing from the project environment (a broken lock or a run outside uv), so the only build test can stop running with a passing suite; the floor run's summary carries a permanent skipped entry.

The rendering test lives under tests/ and opens with a module-level pytest.skip(allow_module_level=True) when sys.version_info is below (3, 11), placed before any import of the build, so the floor run collects it and reports it skipped. The exclusion keys on the interpreter version, matching pyproject.toml's requires-python; nothing outside the test file changes. Self-contained in the test file with no command or documentation change, and under the pinned interpreter it never skips, so a missing PyYAML there fails loudly instead of hiding the test. The 3.11 threshold is a second copy of requires-python that must be kept in step by hand, the skip must stand above the import or collection errors on 3.9, and the floor run's summary carries a permanent skipped entry.

The rendering test lives under tests/, and tests/conftest.py adds its file to collect_ignore (or answers pytest_ignore_collect for it) when the interpreter is below 3.11, so the floor run never collects or imports it and reports nothing for it. Both pytest commands, pyproject.toml, and the test file itself stay free of any version check. The test file stays clean and the floor run's output carries no skip noise; the one rule that keeps build tests off the floor sits in the suite's shared configuration, where a later build test can be added to it. The exclusion is invisible from the test file and from the floor run's output, so a reader of either cannot tell the test is excluded, and the conftest.py that today documents itself as serving the two core/tools/ tools gains a concern about the build; a file name in collect_ignore silently stops matching if the test is renamed.

The rendering test lives in its own directory outside tests/ (for example a build-test directory beside it), which pyproject.toml's testpaths gains so the bare pinned `uv run pytest` collects both, while the floor command is changed to name tests/ explicitly (`uv run --no-project --python 3.9 --with pytest pytest tests`) in drift-gate.yml, CLAUDE.md's Commands, and CONTRIBUTING.md. The split is structural: the build test and the 3.9-portable tool tests never share a directory or conftest.py, and the floor command states on its face exactly what the floor run covers, with no skip logic anywhere. The floor command is changed in three places and a floor run written without the explicit path (the old command) collects the build test and fails with an import error; a second test root departs from the one flat tests/ layout CLAUDE.md describes.

The rendering test lives in its own directory outside tests/, which pyproject.toml's testpaths does not include, so the floor run is untouched and the pinned command is extended to name both directories (`uv run pytest tests <build-test dir>`) in drift-gate.yml, CLAUDE.md's Commands, and CONTRIBUTING.md. The floor run's command and collection stay exactly as they are, so the 3.9 promise is checked by the same line it always was, and no skip or collection rule exists anywhere. A bare `uv run pytest`, the habitual pinned command, silently omits the build test, so the test runs only where the extended command was written; the pinned command changes in three places.

The rendering test lives under tests/ with no version or import check, and the floor command gains `--ignore=tests/<build test file>` in drift-gate.yml, CLAUDE.md's Commands, and CONTRIBUTING.md; pyproject.toml, conftest.py, and the pinned command stay unchanged. The test file and suite configuration carry no exclusion logic, the pinned run needs no change, and the floor command names exactly what it leaves out. The exclusion lives in a command copied into three places, each naming the test file by path, so a rename or a second build test needs all three edited, and anyone running the floor suite from memory without the flag hits an import error.

alternative.id: Build via uv in both runs

open-question.alternative: No exclusion: the rendering test stays under tests/ and runs under both interpreters, but reaches the build only by invoking it as a subprocess through `uv run scripts/build_hosts.py` (or `uv run python` on a driver), so the build code always executes under the project's pinned interpreter with PyYAML whichever interpreter runs the suite. Commands, pyproject.toml, and conftest.py stay unchanged. No skip, collection rule, or command change exists anywhere, and the floor run never carries an excluded or skipped entry, while the build itself still runs only under the pinned interpreter. Viable only if the test reaches the build as a subprocess (the build-test-shape axis); the test depends on uv being on PATH inside pytest, runs the build twice per CI job, and reads against the goal's wording that the test itself runs under the pinned interpreter.

No exclusion: the build's tomllib and yaml imports move inside the functions that load settings and frontmatter, so the module and its slot-filling step import under Python 3.9, and the rendering test, exercising only that step, runs unskipped in both the pinned and the floor run. Commands, pyproject.toml, and conftest.py stay unchanged. One suite, one command pair, and no exclusion mechanism of any kind; the slot-filling logic is also checked at the floor. Viable only if the test reaches just the slot-filling step through an import (the build-test-shape axis); it reshapes the build's imports for a test and extends a 3.9 compatibility burden to build tooling that pyproject.toml deliberately pins to 3.11+, where a later 3.10+ construct in the build would break the floor run.

open-question.question: Four capability-conditional passages of the alternatives pass are to become slots: the opening paragraph's "where the host allows it", the two repair branches of sub-step e, and the repair-wait sentence. How are they divided into slots (one slot per passage, one slot for the whole repair sub-step, or folded into the existing ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY), and, since a slot value may carry no other placeholder, what becomes of the AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT slots that are used only inside those branches? (The two choices constrain each other, so both are asked together.)
open-question.alternative: Division: one new slot per passage, four in all: the opening paragraph's concurrency phrase, the continue-session branch, the re-dispatch branch, and the repair-wait sentence, with the sub-step e lead-in ("whichever of these two branches the host supports, in this order") reworded in core to name no capability. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY stays as it is. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are removed from all three definitions and their wording is written literally inside each host's branch values, as ALTERNATIVES_DISPATCH already writes the `Agent` tool literally. The build is unchanged apart from the milestone's file-backed values. Each slot replaces exactly the text that varies, so sub-step e keeps its present shape in core and every host value is small and local to the sentence it fills, with no build rule relaxed. Core fixes a two-branch skeleton for every host, so a host whose own mechanism has only one repair path renders an empty or awkward bullet, and the tool name is repeated across two values per host; whether every host has both branches depends on the per-host value-sourcing questions.

Division: the same four per-passage slots as the inline option, with the sub-step e lead-in reworded to name no capability and ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY unchanged. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are kept, and the build is changed so a slot value may carry another declared slot placeholder: slot filling runs until no declared placeholder remains (refusing a cycle), and the slot-declaration check counts a slot used only inside another slot's value as used. The tool and agent names stay defined once per host and shared by both branch values, so no wording is duplicated and the existing eight slots survive unchanged. It relaxes a deliberate build rule (a value may carry only `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}`) and adds a recursive fill, cycle handling, and a changed slot-declaration check for the sake of two short phrases, all of which the new rendering test must then cover.

Division: two new slots. The opening phrase gets its own slot; one repair slot holds the sub-step e lead-in, both branches as the host has them, and the repair-wait sentence, with sub-step e reordered in core so that text is contiguous ahead of the fixed corrective message, its fill rule, and the one-repair cap, which stay in core. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY stays as it is. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are retired and written literally inside each host's repair value. Each host states its whole repair mechanism in one value, with as many branches as it really has, so no host inherits another's two-branch structure, while the host-neutral corrective message and cap stay single-sourced. Sub-step e must be reordered and the repair value grows to a multi-line paragraph per host that repeats shared phrasing (the same-path landing, the last-line verdict) unless that is carefully left in core.

Division: the opening phrase as its own slot and one repair slot holding the lead-in, the branches, and the repair-wait sentence, with sub-step e reordered so the fixed corrective message, fill rule, and cap stay in core. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are kept, used inside the repair value, with the build changed to fill slot placeholders inside slot values (repeated until none remain, refusing cycles) and the slot-declaration check counting such use. Gives each host one coherent repair paragraph while keeping the tool and agent names as named, separately commented values per host. Pays the build change for nesting even though both names now occur inside a single value per host, where a literal would cost nothing in duplication.

Division: one new slot for the repair branches (the sub-step e lead-in and both branches as the host has them); the repair-wait sentence is folded into ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY, whose per-host value then says how both first dispatches and repairs are waited on, leaving a host-neutral pointer in sub-step e; the opening phrase is reworded in core to defer to the paragraph opening step 3 rather than slotted. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are retired and written literally into each host's repair value. Puts each concern in one place per host, collection and waiting in the concurrency paragraph that already owns them and repair paths in one value, adding only one slot. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY grows further (already thirteen to twenty lines) and must now describe the repair wait before the reader reaches sub-step e, and the intro no longer says how the dispatches run without a forward reference.

Division: no new slot. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY absorbs the repair branches and the repair wait, so each host's step-3 opening paragraph states how it dispatches, waits, and repairs; sub-step e in core keeps only the trigger (repair every refused file at once), the fixed corrective message, its fill rule, and the one-repair cap; the opening phrase is reworded in core to defer to step 3. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are retired and their wording written literally into each host's concurrency value. Fewest slots: every host-dependent behaviour of the pass lives in one value per host, so a host's whole mechanism can be read and rewritten against a hands-on check in one place. The one paragraph becomes a large multi-topic value that describes repairs before the step that triggers them, splitting the repair procedure between step 3's opening and sub-step e and making the skill harder to follow in order.

Division: only the conditional clauses become slots: the opening phrase, the sub-step e lead-in, each branch's condition clause ("Where the host can continue…", "Where the host cannot…"), and the repair-wait sentence's condition, while the branch bodies stay in core. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY stays as it is. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT stay exactly as they are, still used in the core branch bodies, with no build change. The smallest edit to core and to the build: existing slots and the value-may-carry-only-PLUGIN_ROOT rule are untouched, and the shared branch wording stays single-sourced. Slot values become sentence fragments that must read grammatically against core text, and a host cannot drop a branch its mechanism lacks, so every tree still renders both repair branches; it works only if every host's value-sourcing outcome keeps both branches.

open-question.question: The new per-host slots need Claude Code values that describe only that host's own mechanism, yet the goal names a hands-on check for Antigravity alone. Where do the Claude Code values come from: lifted from the arm of today's capability-conditional prose that applies to it, rewritten from a hands-on check of Claude Code as well, or taken from its documentation alone?

The new per-host slots need Codex values for the repair branches and repair wait, which today's Codex definition does not cover. Where do those values come from: derived from Codex's documentation as the existing Codex values were, or rewritten from a hands-on check against the locally installed codex as well?
open-question.alternative: The Codex values for the repair branches and the repair wait are lifted from what the repository already holds: the current Codex ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY value (which already keeps a round's refused agents open "so repair by continuation still reaches them" and gives the repair set its own wait_agent call and batch) and the documentation findings milestone 40 recorded on 2026-10-01. No documentation is fetched again and the installed codex is not run or inspected. The eight existing Codex values stay as they are. Costs no research at all, and the repair-wait value is close to a copy of a sentence the Codex definition already commits to, so the new values cannot contradict the existing ones. Milestone 40 recorded that the documentation does not say whether a finished subagent thread accepts a follow-up message, so the continuation branch would carry that unverified assumption forward, and nothing on record names the tool a follow-up is sent with.

The Codex values are derived from Codex's public documentation fetched again in this milestone, the way the existing Codex values were. Where the documentation is silent (as it was on following up a finished subagent), the value follows its most plausible reading and keeps the continuation branch the current Codex ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY already assumes. The installed codex is not run or inspected, and the eight existing Codex values stay as they are. Keeps one provenance for every Codex value, documentation, as milestone 40 established, at the cost of one fetch, and picks up anything the documentation has added since 2026-10-01. Leaves the Codex repair wording resting on an unconfirmed reading while the Antigravity values in the same milestone are checked by hand, so the one tree whose repair mechanism the milestone exists to pin down may still describe a mechanism that does not work.

The Codex values are derived from Codex's public documentation (fetched again) and describe only what it states: the repair is a fresh re-dispatch with the spawn_agent tool, and the continuation branch is dropped from the Codex tree because no documentation confirms that a finished subagent accepts a follow-up. The Codex ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY value's clause keeping refused agents open for continuation is reworded to match. The installed codex is not run or inspected. Every Codex sentence rests on a documented mechanism, with no unverified claim and no live run, and re-dispatch is the branch milestone 40 already relies on for first dispatches. Gives up continuation's reuse of the agent's context on a repair even if Codex does support it, and edits an existing Codex value the milestone otherwise has no reason to touch; how the reworded wait fits depends on how the repair passages are divided into slots.

The Codex values are derived from Codex's documentation together with a static read of the locally installed codex (codex-cli 0.159.3): its help text and the agent tool names and descriptions embedded in the binary, which include spawn_agent, wait_agent, close_agent, send_input, send_message, followup_task, and resume_agent. No session is launched and no subagent is dispatched. The eight existing Codex values stay as they are. Names the actual follow-up tool the installed build exposes, which the documentation did not, without spending a model run or installing the plugin into a Codex session. A tool's presence in the binary shows neither that it reaches a finished subagent, nor that it is enabled by default rather than behind a feature flag, nor how wait_agent behaves on a repair set, so the continuation branch is still unconfirmed in behaviour.

The Codex values for the repair branches and the repair wait are rewritten from Codex's documentation plus a hands-on run of the locally installed codex (codex-cli 0.159.3) that exercises exactly what those values describe: sending a follow-up to a finished subagent, re-spawning a fresh generic subagent, and waiting with wait_agent on a repair set alone. The eight existing Codex values are not re-checked and stay as they are unless the run contradicts one the new values depend on. Settles the one point milestone 40 left open, whether a finished Codex subagent accepts a follow-up, with direct evidence, and gives the Codex repair wording the same footing the goal gives Antigravity's, at the smallest scope that achieves it. Costs a live session with model calls and the plugin or a stand-in agent file installed, ties the values to one Codex release, and leaves the existing Codex values on documentation-only footing, so the tree mixes two kinds of provenance.

Every Codex slot value, the new repair-branch and repair-wait values and the eight existing ones (AGENTS.md as the context file, the generic subagent reading the plugin's agent file, the agents.max_threads cap and its default of 6, wait_agent rounds, close_agent), is rewritten from Codex's documentation plus a hands-on run of the locally installed codex (codex-cli 0.159.3) covering dispatch, waiting, continuing an agent, and the context file, mirroring the check the goal names for Antigravity. Puts the whole Codex tree on one checked footing, catching any drift since the 2026-10-01 documentation fetch (such as the agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session rename the existing value already hedges on), so no Codex value is left as an unconfirmed reading. Widens the milestone beyond its goal, which names a hands-on check for Antigravity alone, and may force rewriting Codex values that nothing else in the milestone touches, with the largest run and the most churn in the committed Codex tree.

open-question.question: The Antigravity slot values are to be rewritten from a hands-on check against the installed agy. Where is that check recorded so a later editor can tell what each value was written against: in the comment above each value in the host definition, in the milestone's decisions only, as a repeatable script kept in the repository, or nowhere beyond the values themselves?
open-question.alternative: Recorded in the Antigravity host definition, per value: the comment above each Antigravity slot value in scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml names the agy version the value was checked against and the observed behaviour it rests on (what dispatch, waiting, continuing an agent, or the context file was seen to do). No separate file, script, or CLAUDE.md entry carries the check. The record sits at the exact place an editor changing a value reads, and it extends the existing convention that each slot comment says why this host's value is what it is, so a value written from observation and one written by inference are told apart at a glance. The version is repeated across every Antigravity comment and nothing checks it, so a value edited later without a re-check keeps a stamp that now overclaims, and a newer agy leaves every stamp silently stale; where a value ends up held in a file rather than inline is a condition on whether a comment can sit above it at all (the inline-versus-file assignment and the file-backed binding form are sibling questions).

Recorded in the Antigravity host definition, once: a single block in the header comment of scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml names the agy version and date of the check and lists what was observed; the per-value comments state only what each value describes and why, in mechanism terms, with no version. A later re-check updates one block rather than every comment, and the definition still carries its own evidence where an editor of it looks first. The stamp covers the whole definition, so a single value edited afterwards without a re-check still reads as checked; an editor must connect a value to the header list by hand rather than seeing its basis beside it.

Recorded in this milestone's directory only: the check's agy version and each observation the values rest on are written out deliberately in the milestone's own record (its Decisions and the completing task's Verified entry in TASKS_DONE.md); the host definition's comments keep describing each value in mechanism terms with no version or reference to the check. Adds nothing to maintain: the record is a committed, dated snapshot that never claims to be current, and git blame on a value leads to the milestone commits that wrote it. An editor reading settings.toml sees no sign that a value was observed or against which agy, and must know to dig through history to find it; the milestone files are not where host-definition editors look.

Recorded in CLAUDE.md: the rewritten "Host wording differences are named slots" invariant states that the Antigravity values were written from a hands-on check, names the agy version, and summarises the observed mechanisms they rest on; the host definition's comments carry no version. CLAUDE.md is already the home of rationale and is read at the start of every session, and today's invariant already explains why the Antigravity value is what it is, so the replacement explanation lands where the old one stood. Puts a volatile tool version and behaviour facts into the invariants file, which is meant to hold lasting design decisions, and separates the evidence from the values it covers so the two can drift apart unnoticed.

Recorded as an executable probe kept in the repository (under scripts/): it runs the installed agy's version, help, and agent-listing commands and checks the strings the Antigravity values rely on, and each Antigravity slot comment points at it; the parts of the check it cannot automate are noted in the script beside the commands. A re-check after an agy update is one command rather than a manual investigation, and the evidence can be reproduced rather than taken on trust. Only the static facts (version, flags, help strings, agent listing) are scriptable; dispatch, waiting, and continuing an agent need a live model session that is nondeterministic, billed, and logged in, so the script proves the least important part; it cannot run in CI where agy is absent, adds an untested script to scripts/, and goes stale as silently as a comment.

Not recorded anywhere deliberately: the rewritten values stand on their own, their comments describe each mechanism and why the value is what it is with no version or reference to the check, and the only trace is whatever the routine completion entry and commit history happen to hold. Makes no claim that can go stale, matches how the Codex values are recorded today (their comments cite the mechanism and no version), and adds no artifact to keep in step with agy. A later editor cannot tell what agy the values were written against or whether a value was observed rather than inferred, which is the very uncertainty that left the Antigravity values unchecked until this milestone.

open-question.question: Antigravity's tree today names CLAUDE.md as the context file, while the agy binary names GEMINI.md and AGENTS.md as its rule files and never CLAUDE.md. If the hands-on check confirms that Antigravity reads more than one project instruction file, which one does the Antigravity tree name as its context file?
open-question.alternative: The Antigravity CONTEXT_FILE value stays "CLAUDE.md", as it is today. Only the comment above it is rewritten so that it no longer claims byte-identity with the Claude Code tree. Every one of the roughly thirty CONTEXT_FILE sites, the bootstrap's created file, and the README template's /init sentence keep naming CLAUDE.md. Nothing changes for existing Antigravity projects. A project that runs both Claude Code and Antigravity keeps one shared context file. The skills read the file explicitly by path, so they work whether or not agy loads it on its own. The agy binary names GEMINI.md, AGENTS.md, and .agents/rules/*.md as rule files and never CLAUDE.md. So the workflow section the bootstrap writes would never reach an Antigravity session's context by itself, and agy's /init would document the project somewhere the skills do not read. It also leaves the Antigravity tree naming another host's instruction file, which contradicts the goal that each tree describes only its own mechanism.

The Antigravity CONTEXT_FILE value becomes "AGENTS.md" at the workspace root. The Antigravity and Codex trees then name the same file. The README template's /init sentence is rewritten to name it too. It is one of agy's documented workspace rule paths, and agy's embedded documentation recommends a consolidated AGENTS.md (with GEMINI.md given as the parenthetical alternative, and rules/AGENTS.md recommended inside plugins). As the cross-tool convention, it lets a project used under both Codex and Antigravity keep one environment-context file and one workflow section. The value stays a plain root-level file name, so every "workspace root" sentence and the bootstrap's "# CONTEXT_FILE" heading read correctly without touching core/. If the hands-on check shows that agy's own /init or project setup writes GEMINI.md, a project documented the Antigravity way would hold its context in a file the skills never read. Existing Antigravity projects whose workflow section sits in CLAUDE.md stop being read, which depends on what the context-file transition question decides.

The Antigravity CONTEXT_FILE value becomes "GEMINI.md" at the workspace root. The README template's /init sentence is rewritten to name it too. It is the instruction file agy names first and the one belonging to Antigravity's own model family, so it is the file most specific to this host. It keeps Antigravity's workflow section apart from any AGENTS.md that other tools or Codex maintain in the same project. A project used under both Codex and Antigravity ends up with two environment-context files and two copies of the workflow section, and the two drift apart. agy's embedded documentation recommends AGENTS.md over it. Existing Antigravity projects whose workflow section sits in CLAUDE.md stop being read, which depends on what the context-file transition question decides.

The Antigravity CONTEXT_FILE value becomes a cairn-owned file under agy's workspace rules directory, for example ".agents/rules/cairn.md". It sits beside the .agents/plugins/cairn install path, and the bootstrap creates it there. Because the value is no longer at the workspace root, the core/ sentences that say "at the workspace root" are reworded so they read correctly for a nested path. agy loads every .agents/rules/*.md file, so the workflow section reaches each session. Cairn also never edits a project instruction file shared with other tools or with the project's own /init output, and all of cairn's Antigravity state stays under .agents/. The file is meant to be both the project's environment context, read by derive-tasks, specify-milestone-starting-state, and the completion procedure, and the home of the workflow section. A cairn-owned rules file would hold only the workflow section, so the skills would find no domain context unless the user moves it there. It also needs core/ edits outside the slot, since "workspace root CONTEXT_FILE" and the "# CONTEXT_FILE" heading assume a root-level file name.

No file name is fixed now. The Antigravity CONTEXT_FILE value is whichever root-level file the hands-on check shows agy's own /init (or its project-documenting step) writes, either GEMINI.md or AGENTS.md. The README template names that same file. It keeps the project's own documentation step and the workflow's reads and writes on one file. This is the same reason the Codex value gives for AGENTS.md ("its /init writes that file"), so the slot comment can state a checked fact rather than a preference. The recorded decision is a rule, not a value, so the file name is settled only when the check runs. If agy has no /init or writes neither file, the rule does not resolve and the question reopens. Existing Antigravity projects whose workflow section sits in CLAUDE.md stop being read, which depends on what the context-file transition question decides.

open-question.question: If the Antigravity context file changes away from CLAUDE.md, is any transition provided for existing Antigravity projects whose CLAUDE.md already carries the workflow section, or does the change apply only to projects bootstrapped after it?
open-question.alternative: The change applies only to projects bootstrapped after it. Existing Antigravity projects get no explicit notice beyond the release's ordinary CHANGELOG entry, no runtime fallback, and no migration step. Their CLAUDE.md is left exactly as it stands, and every skill reads the new context file from the release that makes the change. It adds no code, prose, or new behaviour to core/ or the Antigravity definition. It matches the project's standing no-migration posture (the pre-split milestones and the question-order change both shipped with no migration step). The Antigravity install base is thin: the only Antigravity copy on this machine is a pre-tool port, and Antigravity's own rule loading never read CLAUDE.md, so the workflow section there was never auto-loaded. An existing Antigravity project silently loses the environment context its CLAUDE.md holds. Skills such as derive-tasks, specify-milestone-starting-state, and the completion procedure then read a missing or bare file and only suggest /init. Re-running the bootstrap does not repair this, because it stops at "Workflow already bootstrapped" whenever milestones/ and the pointer exist. The option only applies if the Antigravity context file actually changes, which the context-file choice question decides.

No runtime change. The release that makes the change carries an explicit transition instruction in the CHANGELOG entry and in the Antigravity README template, which today tells users to run /init into CLAUDE.md. The instruction tells existing Antigravity users to move or copy their CLAUDE.md content, both the environment context and the ## Milestone Workflow section, into the new context file, or to link the new file to it. Existing users get a clear, one-time remedy at almost no cost: a few sentences in files the release already touches, with no change to any skill or to the bootstrap's run-once contract, and with the user rather than a skill deciding what to do with their own CLAUDE.md. It only helps users who read the release notes or the README. A user who upgrades without reading them still gets the silent context loss of the forward-only option. Wording about another file also puts transition prose into the Antigravity tree's own templates, whose scope under the other-host naming rule is a sibling question.

init-milestone-base-workflow is changed for every host so that an already-bootstrapped project whose context file is missing or lacks the ## Milestone Workflow section is not stopped as "already bootstrapped". Instead the skill runs its step 6 (create the file or append the section) and commits that alone. The release instruction tells existing Antigravity users to re-run the bootstrap and then /init to document their environment in the new file. CLAUDE.md is left untouched. It gives existing projects a supported, committed path to a correct new context file through a skill they already know, with the workflow section written by the same step that writes it for new projects. The bootstrap also becomes able to repair a context file deleted or renamed for any other reason. It changes the bootstrap's "already initialized" stop condition and its no-op line for every host, to serve one host's transition. It restores only the workflow section, not the environment context, so the user still has to run /init or move content by hand. And it still depends on the user reading the instruction.

The skills that read the context file in the Antigravity tree read the new file and fall back to CLAUDE.md when the new file is absent. The fallback is permanent and has no removal date. It is expressed through the Antigravity slot values or an added slot, since CONTEXT_FILE today is a single file name used at about thirty sites, including the bootstrap's file heading. The bootstrap still creates or extends only the new file, and no instruction is needed for the fallback to work. Existing projects keep working with no action and no reading required: their environment context in CLAUDE.md keeps reaching every skill that reads it, while new projects get the new file from the start. It puts a second file name and conditional wording into every context-file site of the Antigravity tree. That reintroduces the capability-conditional branching this milestone exists to remove, and it keeps a file name Antigravity itself never loads in its runtime prose. The CONTEXT_FILE slot's single-name shape would have to change or a new slot would be needed, which ties this option to how the slot granularity is settled.

The Antigravity tree's bootstrap gains a one-time migration step. When the new context file is absent and CLAUDE.md carries the ## Milestone Workflow section, it copies or moves CLAUDE.md's content into the new file and commits the result under the bootstrap's subject. The "already bootstrapped" stop is relaxed to let this step run, and no instruction beyond pointing users at a re-run is given. It carries both the workflow section and the environment context across in one committed step, so no context is lost and the user does not have to edit files by hand. It contradicts the bootstrap's own rule never to document the project's environment context in the context file itself. It may move content a user still wants under CLAUDE.md for another host. It adds host-specific migration behaviour that core/ has no slot shape for, and it reverses the project's consistent no-migration posture, all for a host with a thin install base. It still runs only if the user re-runs the bootstrap.

open-question.question: If the hands-on check shows that Antigravity loads a plugin's agents only through a manifest or frontmatter fields the agent files do not carry today, does this milestone add what Antigravity needs to its host definition, or do the Antigravity slot values describe a generic-subagent fallback as the Codex ones do?

alternative.id: Native loading via a new build key

open-question.alternative: This milestone makes Antigravity load the two agents natively, adding whatever the hands-on check shows it needs. A required manifest (such as a root-level agents.json) is added as a template file beside plugin.json in scripts/hosts/antigravity/. Required frontmatter fields (such as subagent or tools) come from a new per-host settings key that adds frontmatter keys to the rendered agent files, the mirror of strip_frontmatter_keys, so the build gains one capability and core/agents/ stays unchanged. The Antigravity dispatch slot values then name the plugin's agents directly, the way the Claude Code values name the cairn: registry names. The Antigravity tree dispatches real named agents with their own definitions, the closest match to the Claude Code behaviour, and the host-specific fields live only in Antigravity's own definition, so no other tree carries or strips them. It widens a milestone about slots into agent-packaging work: a new settings key every definition must declare (empty for Claude Code and Codex), with its validation, and a native loading path that only the hands-on check can confirm, so a wrong reading of agy's loader leaves agents that never load.

alternative.id: Native loading via fields in core

open-question.alternative: This milestone makes Antigravity load the two agents natively. A required manifest is added as a template beside plugin.json, as in the build-key route. Required frontmatter fields are written into the two core/agents/ files themselves, and the Claude Code and Codex definitions list those keys in their strip_frontmatter_keys, the way Antigravity and Codex strip color today, so the build needs no new capability. The Antigravity dispatch slot values name the plugin's agents directly. Native named agents on Antigravity with no change to the build's key schema or code, reusing the one frontmatter mechanism the build already has. core/ comes to carry one host's loading fields that every other host must remember to strip, the reverse of the milestone's direction toward each host's differences living in its own definition, and a field name Claude Code also reads (tools) would restrict that host's agents if a strip were ever missed.

This milestone adds native loading only when the hands-on check shows that a file the build can already emit is enough: a manifest template beside plugin.json, or a relocation through the existing layout and renames. If agy needs frontmatter fields the build cannot add today, nothing is added for loading and the Antigravity slot values describe the generic-subagent fallback instead, a subagent told to read the plugin's agent file by its plugin-root path, as the Codex values do. The build's key schema and code stay as the rest of the milestone leaves them either way. It takes native agents where they are cheap and caps the cost where they are not, so the milestone never grows a build capability for loading alone. The outcome, and so the shape of the Antigravity values and docs, is left to whatever the check finds, and on the fallback path a later milestone still faces the same choice; how the check and its result are recorded is the Hands-on check record question's to settle.

This milestone adds nothing to the Antigravity definition for agent loading: no manifest template, no frontmatter field, no build change. The Antigravity slot values describe dispatching agy's generic subagent (through invoke_subagent or whatever the check shows is its dispatch tool) told to read and follow the plugin's agent file by its plugin-root path, the same shape as the Codex values. Native loading is not ruled out but is left out of scope for a later milestone. The smallest change, already proven in shape by the Codex tree, and it keeps the milestone to slot values and their wording, with the agent files and the build untouched by loading concerns. Antigravity runs the agents' definitions as instructions inside a generic subagent rather than as named agents, so any per-agent setting agy would honour natively (model, tool limits) is lost, and the installed plugin keeps shipping agent files agy itself never loads.

This milestone adds nothing to the Antigravity definition for agent loading. Instead the Antigravity slot values tell the runner to define each agent at run time through agy's define_subagent mechanism from the plugin's agent file, once per run before the first dispatch, and then dispatch that defined subagent by name. The agent files stay the single source, read from the plugin-root path, and the build is unchanged. It yields a named subagent carrying the agent file as its own definition, closer to native loading than a generic subagent told to read a file, without any manifest, frontmatter field, or build capability. It rests on define_subagent, which is known only from strings embedded in the agy binary and must be confirmed by the hands-on check, and it adds a define step to every dispatching run, a step with no counterpart on the other hosts that the slot values must describe in full.

open-question.question: The new development rule says a rendered tree must never name another host's mechanism. Does it cover only the files rendered from core/, or also the host's own templates (README, CONTRIBUTING pointer, manifest) in the same tree?

Today no slot value names a host, in keeping with the rule that runtime files name no host. Once a slot value describes one host's own mechanism, may it name that host (for example its tool by the host's name), or must it still describe the mechanism without naming the host?

CONTRIBUTING.md's Development section describes settings.toml without its [slots] table or plugin_dir and would say nothing of file-backed values or the new rule. Is that section rewritten in this milestone alongside CLAUDE.md and docs/, or left out of scope?
open-question.alternative: CONTRIBUTING.md is not edited in this milestone. Its Development section keeps describing settings.toml as the plugin-root literal, frontmatter keys to strip, renames, excluded paths, and the layout, keeps its partial check list, and keeps saying the pytest suite covers the tools under core/tools/ and runs under both interpreters. The new rule and the file-backed values are written down only in CLAUDE.md, docs/, and the build script's docstring. The gap is recorded under Out of Scope, deferred to a later documentation pass rather than declared permanent. Keeps the milestone to its stated surfaces (the build, core/, the host definitions, CLAUDE.md, docs/) and adds no third prose description of the build that has to agree with the docstring and CLAUDE.md. CLAUDE.md sends readers to CONTRIBUTING.md ## Development for the build loop and both test runs, so after this milestone that section would describe a settings.toml with no slots and a suite whose every test runs on both interpreters, both of which are then false or incomplete for anyone adding a host, a slot, or a build test.

Only what this milestone itself changes is written into the section: the settings.toml sentence gains the slot values a definition supplies, inline in its [slots] table or held in files, and the test paragraph says the suite now includes a rendering test of the build that runs under the pinned interpreter only. The older omissions (plugin_dir, the slot-declaration and host-name-in-core checks, the rest of the check list) are left as they stand, and the new development rule is not stated in CONTRIBUTING.md; it lives in CLAUDE.md and docs/ only. The smallest edit that keeps the section from becoming newly wrong: every sentence the milestone would falsify is fixed and nothing outside the milestone's own changes is touched. The section stays knowingly incomplete on pre-existing facts (plugin_dir, half the checks), and a human contributor who reads CONTRIBUTING.md but not CLAUDE.md never learns that a rendered tree must not name another host's mechanism; the test-paragraph wording also depends on how the floor run excludes the build test, which the floor-run question owns.

The same targeted edit as above (slot values inline or file-backed, the pinned-only build rendering test), plus the new development rule stated for contributors in the section: host differences reach core/ as named slots rather than capability-conditional prose, and a rendered tree never names another host's mechanism. The older omissions (plugin_dir, the slot-declaration and host-name-in-core checks, the rest of the check list) are left as they stand. Every change this milestone makes, the rule included, reaches the contributor guide that outside contributors are pointed to, without widening the edit into a catch-up of facts the milestone did not change. The rule gains a second home beside CLAUDE.md that must be kept in agreement with it, and what the rule covers depends on the other-host rule scope question; the pre-existing gaps remain, so the section is still not a complete account of settings.toml or the checks.

The section's factual description is brought fully up to date: settings.toml is described with every key it holds, plugin_dir and the [slots] table included, with slot values inline or file-backed; the check list names every check the build runs, slot-declaration and host-name-in-core included; and the test paragraph covers the pinned-only build rendering test. The new development rule is not stated in CONTRIBUTING.md; it lives in CLAUDE.md and docs/ only. The section becomes an accurate, complete description of the build again in one pass, closing the gaps that predate this milestone along with the ones it creates, while keeping rules in CLAUDE.md. Widens the milestone into documentation debt it did not create, and re-enumerates settings keys and checks that the build script's docstring already lists, so every future key or check must be added in two places or the section drifts again; human contributors still do not see the rule.

The full factual catch-up above (every settings.toml key including plugin_dir and [slots] with inline or file-backed values, every build check including slot-declaration and host-name-in-core, the pinned-only build rendering test), plus the new development rule stated for contributors: host differences reach core/ as named slots rather than capability-conditional prose, and a rendered tree never names another host's mechanism. CONTRIBUTING.md ## Development becomes a complete, current guide to adding a host or a slot, rule included, matching what CLAUDE.md promises the section holds. The largest edit: it both duplicates the docstring's enumerations and gives the rule a second home beside CLAUDE.md, so three places must agree on settings keys and checks and two on the rule, and the rule's wording depends on the other-host rule scope question.

The section stops enumerating: its settings.toml sentence and check list are replaced by a short description of what a host definition is (settings plus templates, wording differences as named slots whose values sit inline or in files) and a pointer to the build script's docstring as the one complete reference for settings keys and checks; the test paragraph covers the pinned-only build rendering test. The new development rule is not stated in CONTRIBUTING.md. Removes the duplicated enumeration that let the section drift in the first place, so later keys and checks need updating only in the docstring that sits beside the code they describe. A contributor must open a Python file's docstring to learn the checks, the docstring must itself be kept current with the file-backed form this milestone adds, and the rule still reaches no one who reads only CONTRIBUTING.md.

The pointer restructure above (a short description of host definitions and slots with inline or file-backed values, the build script's docstring named as the complete reference for settings keys and checks, the pinned-only build rendering test in the test paragraph), plus the new development rule stated for contributors: host differences reach core/ as named slots rather than capability-conditional prose, and a rendered tree never names another host's mechanism. The section carries the concepts and the rule a contributor needs to make a host-dependent change correctly while delegating every list that changes with the code to the docstring, so it says more that matters and has less to keep in sync. Reshapes the section beyond what the milestone strictly requires, gives the rule a second home beside CLAUDE.md, and relies on the docstring being complete and current; the rule's wording depends on the other-host rule scope question.

open-question.question: docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md lists three --effort values for Antigravity while the installed agy --help lists five. Does this milestone correct that page's Antigravity command-line facts from the same hands-on check, or is that left out of scope?
